lessons.title: Photosynthesis and limiting factors
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Biology — Nutrition in plants: photosynthesis, limiting factors, starch test (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original text written for the GCE O Level Biology syllabus; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Write the word and balanced chemical equations for photosynthesis.
Explain the effect of light intensity, carbon dioxide and temperature on the rate of photosynthesis.
Describe and explain the starch test on a leaf.

blocks.title: Photosynthesis
blocks.md:
**Photosynthesis** is the process by which green plants make carbohydrates (glucose) from **carbon dioxide** and **water**, using **light energy** absorbed by **chlorophyll**. **Oxygen** is released as a by-product.

It takes place mainly in the chloroplasts of the **palisade mesophyll** cells of the leaf. Light energy is converted into chemical energy stored in glucose.

blocks.title: Word equation
blocks.md: Light energy and chlorophyll are the **conditions**: write them above and below the arrow in your answer.

blocks.title: Balanced chemical equation
blocks.md: Six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water give one molecule of glucose and six of oxygen (in light, with chlorophyll). Check: 6 C, 12 H and 18 O atoms on each side.

blocks.title: What the plant does with glucose
blocks.md:
- Uses it in **respiration** to release energy.
- Converts it to **starch** for storage (starch is insoluble).
- Converts it to **sucrose** for transport in the phloem.
- Uses it to make **cellulose** for cell walls.
- Combines it with nitrates (from the soil) to make **amino acids** and proteins.

blocks.title: Limiting factor
blocks.md:
A **limiting factor** is the factor in shortest supply, which therefore limits the rate of a process.

For photosynthesis the main limiting factors are **light intensity**, **carbon dioxide concentration** and **temperature** (temperature acts through the enzymes).

blocks.caption: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity, at two carbon dioxide concentrations (constant temperature).
blocks.alt: Two curves rise from zero and then level off. The curve at high carbon dioxide levels off at about 10 units, the curve at low carbon dioxide levels off lower, at about 6 units.

blocks.title: Reading the graph
blocks.md:
- At **A** (steep part), the rate rises when light increases: **light intensity** is the limiting factor.
- At **B** (plateau), more light has no effect: another factor, here **carbon dioxide** (or temperature), is limiting.
- Raising the CO2 concentration raises the plateau: CO2 was limiting.

Farmers use this in greenhouses by adding lighting, carbon dioxide or heat.

blocks.title: Method: testing a leaf for starch
blocks.md:
1. Destarch the plant first by leaving it in the dark for 48 hours.
2. Boil the leaf in water for about 1 minute: this kills the cells and stops all reactions.
3. Put it in hot ethanol in a water bath (flame off, ethanol is flammable): this removes the chlorophyll.
4. Rinse in warm water: this softens the brittle leaf.
5. Spread it on a white tile and add iodine solution: **blue-black** = starch present; **orange-brown** = no starch.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: a variegated leaf
blocks.statement: A destarched plant with variegated leaves (green centre, white edges) is left in sunlight for 6 hours. A leaf is then tested with iodine solution. The result is shown. What does the experiment show?

steps.md: The two parts of the leaf received the **same light**, the same CO2 and the same water. The only difference is the presence of **chlorophyll** (green part only).
The formerly green part turns **blue-black**: starch is present, so photosynthesis took place there.
The formerly white part stays **orange-brown**: no starch, so no photosynthesis without chlorophyll.
The plant was destarched first, so any starch found must have been made during the 6 hours of light.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: pondweed and a lamp
blocks.statement: A piece of pondweed is placed in water with a lamp at different distances. At 40 cm it gives 12 bubbles per minute; at 20 cm, 30 bubbles per minute; at 10 cm, 30 bubbles per minute. Explain these results.

steps.md: The bubbles are **oxygen**, a product of photosynthesis: counting them per minute measures the **rate**.
From 40 cm to 20 cm, the light is more intense and the rate rises from 12 to 30 bubbles per minute: **light intensity** was the limiting factor.
From 20 cm to 10 cm, the light is even more intense but the rate stays at 30: light is **no longer** limiting.
Another factor now limits the rate: most likely the **carbon dioxide** concentration in the water, or the temperature.

blocks.answer: **Light limits the rate at low intensity; above a certain intensity, carbon dioxide (or temperature) becomes the limiting factor.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying plants get their food from the soil: they absorb water and mineral salts, but **make** their food.
- Forgetting that plants **respire** day and night, not only in the dark.
- Writing that chlorophyll is used up: it is not a reactant.
- Saying iodine tests for glucose: it tests for **starch**.
- Unbalanced equation: there are **6** O2 molecules, not 3 or 12.

items: Almost all the oxygen in the air we breathe was released by photosynthesis in plants and algae.
In Cameroon, cocoa trees grow well under the shade of taller forest trees: their leaves reach maximum photosynthesis at fairly low light intensities.

reviewNotes: The remark that cocoa leaves saturate at relatively low light intensity is a general agronomic statement: a teacher should confirm it or remove it.

lessons.title: Human digestion and enzymes
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Biology — Nutrition in humans: alimentary canal, digestive enzymes, properties of enzymes (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original text written for the GCE O Level Biology syllabus; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define digestion and describe the role of the main organs of the alimentary canal.
Name the main digestive enzymes, their substrates and their products.
Explain the effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity.

blocks.title: Digestion
blocks.md:
**Digestion** is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be **absorbed** into the blood.

- **Mechanical digestion**: teeth chew the food and the stomach churns it; this increases the surface area.
- **Chemical digestion**: enzymes break the chemical bonds in large molecules.

blocks.title: Enzymes
blocks.md:
An **enzyme** is a protein that acts as a **biological catalyst**: it speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.

- Each enzyme is **specific**: it acts on one substrate only (lock-and-key model).
- It works best at an **optimum temperature** (about 37 °C in humans) and an optimum **pH**.
- High temperatures **denature** it: the active site changes shape permanently.

blocks.title: The main digestive enzymes
blocks.md:
- **Amylase** (salivary glands, pancreas): starch → maltose.
- **Maltase** (small intestine): maltose → glucose.
- **Proteases**, such as **pepsin** (stomach) and **trypsin** (pancreas): proteins → polypeptides → amino acids.
- **Lipase** (pancreas): fats → fatty acids and glycerol.

blocks.title: Path of food through the alimentary canal
blocks.md:
- **Mouth**: chewing; saliva with amylase.
- **Oesophagus**: food moved down by **peristalsis**.
- **Stomach**: hydrochloric acid (pH about 2) kills bacteria; pepsin digests proteins.
- **Duodenum**: receives pancreatic juice and **bile**.
- **Ileum**: digestion is completed and products are **absorbed** through the villi.
- **Colon**: water is absorbed. **Rectum/anus**: faeces are egested.

blocks.title: Bile is not an enzyme
blocks.md: Bile is made in the **liver** and stored in the **gall bladder**. It **emulsifies** fats (breaks them into small droplets, giving lipase a larger surface area) and **neutralises** the stomach acid. It does not break any chemical bond.

blocks.caption: Activity of a human enzyme against temperature: the optimum is about 37 °C; above it the enzyme is denatured.
blocks.alt: A curve rises slowly from 0 to a peak at 37 °C, then falls steeply to nearly zero by about 55 °C.

blocks.title: Method: answering an enzyme experiment question
blocks.md:
1. Identify the **variable changed** (temperature, pH...) and what is measured.
2. Describe the trend with figures from the data.
3. Give the **optimum** (highest rate or shortest time).
4. Explain: below the optimum, molecules have less kinetic energy (fewer collisions); above it, the enzyme is **denatured**.
5. Name the variables that must be kept constant (fair test).

blocks.title: Worked example 1: amylase at three temperatures
blocks.statement: Three tubes each contain starch solution and amylase. They are kept at 10 °C, 37 °C and 80 °C. After 10 minutes, a drop from each is tested with iodine: 10 °C blue-black; 37 °C orange-brown; 80 °C blue-black. Explain the results.

steps.md: Iodine turns **blue-black** with starch. **Orange-brown** means no starch is left: it has all been digested to maltose.
At **37 °C** (near the optimum), amylase has digested all the starch in 10 minutes.
At **10 °C**, amylase works only slowly (low kinetic energy, few collisions): starch remains. The enzyme is inactive but not destroyed.
At **80 °C**, amylase is **denatured**: its active site has changed shape, so it can no longer digest starch, even if cooled.

blocks.answer: **Amylase works best near 37 °C; it is slowed down at 10 °C and denatured at 80 °C.**

blocks.title: Worked example 2: enzymes and pH
blocks.statement: The graph shows the activity of two digestive enzymes, X and Y, at different pH values. Which one could be pepsin? Explain.

steps.md: Read the optimum of each curve at its peak: enzyme **X** has an optimum pH of about **2**; enzyme **Y** about **7**.
The stomach contains hydrochloric acid, so its pH is about 2 (acidic). Pepsin works in the stomach.
Enzyme Y works best at neutral pH, like salivary amylase in the mouth.

blocks.answer: **X could be pepsin: its optimum pH (about 2) matches the acid conditions of the stomach.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying enzymes are "killed": they are not alive; they are **denatured**.
- Saying low temperature denatures an enzyme: cold only **slows** it down.
- Calling bile an enzyme.
- Forgetting that absorption happens mainly in the **ileum**, not the stomach.
- Mixing up the products: starch gives maltose (then glucose), proteins give amino acids, fats give fatty acids and glycerol.

items: The inner wall of the ileum is covered with millions of villi, which give it a very large surface area for absorption.
Washing powders called "biological" contain enzymes (proteases and lipases) that remove food and grease stains at low temperatures.

reviewNotes: Check whether the syllabus names trypsin and maltase explicitly or only the enzyme groups (amylase, protease, lipase).

exercises.prompt: Which gas is released by a green leaf during photosynthesis?
exercises.explanation: Oxygen is the by-product of photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide is taken in as a raw material.
mistakes: Confusing the raw material (CO2) with the product (O2).
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: True or false: according to the balanced equation, six molecules of carbon dioxide are needed to make one molecule of glucose.
exercises.explanation: True: $6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$. Glucose contains six carbon atoms, each coming from one CO2 molecule.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Match each step of the starch test with its reason.
pairs: Kills the cells and stops reactions
Place the leaf in hot ethanol
Rinse the leaf in warm water
exercises.explanation: Water kills the cells; ethanol dissolves the chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen; warm water softens the leaf made brittle by ethanol; iodine turns blue-black with starch.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: The graph shows the rate of photosynthesis of a plant at 25 °C and 0.04 % carbon dioxide. Which factor is most likely to limit the rate at point P?
choices: The number of leaves on the plant
exercises.explanation: At P the curve is flat: more light no longer increases the rate, so light is not limiting. At 0.04 % (the level in air), carbon dioxide is the most likely limiting factor.
exercises.method: Rising part: the factor on the x-axis is limiting. Plateau: another factor is limiting.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: When sodium hydrogencarbonate (a source of CO2) is added to the water, the rate of bubbling of a pondweed rises from 20 to 30 bubbles per minute. Calculate the percentage increase in the rate.
exercises.explanation: Increase = 30 − 20 = 10 bubbles per minute. Percentage increase = 10 ÷ 20 × 100 = 50 %.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt:
A student places a piece of pondweed in a test tube of water at 25 °C and counts the bubbles released in 2 minutes with a lamp at different distances.

- 5 cm: 124 bubbles
- 10 cm: 124 bubbles
- 20 cm: 80 bubbles
- 40 cm: 28 bubbles
exercises.method: Use figures from the data; always say which factor is limiting and why.
mistakes: Forgetting to divide by 2 to get a rate per minute.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.prompt: Which gas makes up most of the bubbles?
parts.explanation: The bubbles are mostly oxygen produced by photosynthesis.

parts.prompt: Calculate the rate of photosynthesis at 20 cm, in bubbles per minute.
parts.explanation: 80 bubbles in 2 minutes: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 bubbles per minute.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes the results from 40 cm to 10 cm?
choices: As the lamp gets closer, the rate increases
As the lamp gets closer, the rate decreases
The rate does not depend on the distance
The rate is highest at 40 cm
parts.explanation: From 40 cm to 10 cm the number of bubbles rises from 28 to 124: the closer the lamp, the brighter the light and the faster the rate.

parts.prompt: Explain why the rate is the same at 5 cm and at 10 cm.
parts.model: Light intensity is no longer the limiting factor (1 mark). Another factor, such as the carbon dioxide concentration or the temperature, now limits the rate (1 mark).
rubric: 1 mark: light is no longer limiting.
1 mark: names another limiting factor (carbon dioxide or temperature).
parts.explanation: At 5 and 10 cm there is plenty of light; the rate is held back by another factor in short supply.

parts.prompt: Why is the tube kept at 25 °C during the whole experiment?
choices: To make it a fair test, since temperature also affects the rate
To kill bacteria in the water
To stop the plant from respiring
parts.explanation: Temperature affects the enzymes of photosynthesis; only the light intensity should change, so the temperature is kept constant.

exercises.prompt: What are the two raw materials of photosynthesis?
exercises.explanation: Carbon dioxide (from the air) and water (from the soil) are the raw materials; glucose and oxygen are the products.

exercises.prompt: What is the role of chlorophyll?
exercises.explanation: Chlorophyll, in the chloroplasts, absorbs light energy used to make glucose.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct balanced equation for photosynthesis?
exercises.explanation: Six CO2 and six H2O give one glucose and six O2. The reverse equation is respiration.

exercises.prompt: Why is a leaf placed in hot ethanol during the starch test?
exercises.explanation: Ethanol dissolves the chlorophyll, so that the colour of the iodine can be seen clearly.

exercises.prompt: On a graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity, the curve levels off. This means that...
exercises.explanation: On the plateau, extra light has no effect: another factor such as CO2 or temperature limits the rate.

exercises.prompt: Match each enzyme with the reaction it catalyses.
exercises.explanation: Enzyme names often come from the substrate: amyl- (starch), malt- (maltose), prote- (protein), lip- (lipid, fat).
exercises.method: Use the first part of the enzyme's name to find its substrate.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Where is bile produced?
exercises.explanation: Bile is produced by the liver and only stored in the gall bladder before being released into the duodenum.
mistakes: Answering "gall bladder": it stores bile but does not make it.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: True or false: bile is an enzyme that digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
exercises.explanation: False. Bile contains no enzyme: it emulsifies fats into small droplets. Lipase then digests them into fatty acids and glycerol.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Amylase solution is boiled, cooled to 37 °C, then mixed with starch solution. After 15 minutes the mixture is tested with iodine. What is the result, and why?
choices: Blue-black, because the amylase was denatured
Orange-brown, because the starch was digested
Blue-black, because 37 °C is too cold for amylase
exercises.explanation: Boiling denatures amylase permanently: cooling it again does not restore its active site. The starch is not digested and iodine turns blue-black.
mistakes: Thinking that the enzyme works again once cooled.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: A tube contains 5.0 g of starch and amylase at 37 °C. After 20 minutes, 2.0 g of starch remain. Calculate the percentage of the starch that has been digested.
exercises.explanation: Starch digested = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 g. Percentage = 3.0 ÷ 5.0 × 100 = 60 %.
mistakes: Giving the percentage remaining (40 %) instead of the percentage digested.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt:
Amylase is mixed with starch solution at different temperatures (same pH). The time taken for all the starch to disappear is recorded.

- 10 °C: 20 minutes
- 25 °C: 8 minutes
- 37 °C: 4 minutes
- 60 °C: starch still present after 30 minutes
exercises.method: Shortest time = fastest rate. Rate = 1 ÷ time.
mistakes: Choosing the temperature with the longest time as the optimum.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.prompt: Among the temperatures tested, at which one does amylase work fastest?
parts.explanation: The starch disappears in the shortest time (4 minutes) at 37 °C.

parts.prompt: The rate of reaction is 1 ÷ time. Calculate the rate at 37 °C.
Explain why the starch is still present at 60 °C.
parts.model: At 60 °C the amylase is denatured (1 mark): the shape of its active site has changed, so starch can no longer fit/bind and is not digested (1 mark).
rubric: 1 mark: the active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits.
parts.explanation: High temperature permanently changes the shape of the enzyme's active site.

parts.prompt: Why is the pH kept the same in every tube?
choices: pH also affects enzyme activity, so it must be controlled for a fair test
pH changes the colour of starch
To stop the starch from dissolving
parts.explanation: Only one variable (temperature) should change; pH also affects enzymes, so it is controlled.

parts.prompt: What is the product of the digestion of starch by amylase?
parts.explanation: Amylase digests starch into maltose; maltase then turns maltose into glucose.

exercises.prompt: What is an enzyme?
choices: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst
A fat that forms cell membranes
A mineral salt used by cells
exercises.explanation: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up.

exercises.prompt: Where are most digested food molecules absorbed?
exercises.explanation: The ileum, lined with villi, absorbs most of the products of digestion. The colon mainly absorbs water.

exercises.prompt: Fats are digested into...
exercises.explanation: Lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

exercises.prompt: What is the main role of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
choices: It kills bacteria and gives pepsin its optimum pH
exercises.explanation: The acid (pH about 2) kills most bacteria in food and provides the acidic conditions pepsin needs.

exercises.prompt: What happens to an enzyme at a temperature well above its optimum?
exercises.explanation: Its active site changes shape permanently: the enzyme is denatured and stops working.

exercises.prompt: Question 2 — Nutrition (6 marks). This question is about photosynthesis in a maize plant and about digestion in humans.
exercises.method: Use biological vocabulary precisely (denatured, active site, limiting factor).
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.prompt: Using the balanced equation for photosynthesis, state how many molecules of oxygen are released for each molecule of glucose made.
parts.explanation: $6CO_2 + 6H_2O \to C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$: six molecules of oxygen per molecule of glucose.

parts.prompt: Which raw material of photosynthesis does the maize plant absorb from the soil?
parts.explanation: Water is absorbed by the root hairs; carbon dioxide enters the leaves from the air.

parts.prompt: In a brightly lit greenhouse at 25 °C, extra lighting does not increase the growth of the plants. Which change is most likely to increase the rate of photosynthesis?
choices: Keeping the plants in the dark
parts.explanation: Light is no longer limiting, so another factor is: carbon dioxide is the most likely one, and raising it increases the rate.

parts.prompt: Which enzyme begins the digestion of proteins in the stomach?
parts.explanation: Pepsin is a protease that works in the acidic conditions of the stomach.

parts.prompt: Explain why salivary amylase stops digesting starch when it is heated to 70 °C.
parts.model: The enzyme is denatured by the high temperature (1 mark); its active site changes shape, so the starch molecule no longer fits and cannot be broken down (1 mark).
rubric: 1 mark: change of shape of the active site, substrate no longer fits.
parts.explanation: Enzymes are proteins: heat above the optimum permanently changes the shape of the active site.
